name: Developing AI Apps and Agents on Azure
audience: Azure AI engineers who build, deploy and manage AI apps and agents with Microsoft Foundry and Python
format: About 40–60 items in 100 minutes, which may include case studies and interactive items; scaled score 1–1000, pass 700. The certification page quotes 120 minutes, which is seat time including instructions and survey; Microsoft gives associate exams without labs 100 minutes of exam time. $165 is the US price; Microsoft prices exams by country. Renew yearly with a free online assessment. This site practises multiple choice and multiple response only.

domains.name: Plan and manage an Azure AI solution
domains.summary: Officially 25–30% of the exam. Choosing models and Foundry services, designing infrastructure and deployments with CI/CD, managing quotas, cost and monitoring (including ingestion quality, index health and relevance), and securing solutions with managed identity, keyless auth, private networking, Foundry RBAC and guardrails.

domains.name: Implement generative AI and agentic solutions
domains.summary: Officially 30–35% of the exam. Connecting apps to a Foundry project, building RAG with Azure AI Search, prompt engineering and function calling, building single and multi-agent solutions with Foundry Agent Service and Microsoft Agent Framework, and evaluating and observing them with tracing, chain-of-thought evaluations and safety signals.

domains.name: Implement computer vision solutions
domains.summary: Officially 10–15% of the exam. Generating and editing images with the gpt-image series, generating and editing video from text and reference media, analysing images and video with Content Understanding, and enforcing visual content policy (watermarks, prohibited symbols, brand usage, inappropriate content).

domains.name: Implement text analysis solutions
domains.summary: Officially 10–15% of the exam. Extracting insights and structured JSON from text with language models and Azure Language (PII, health, entities), translation, and speech solutions: speech-to-text, text-to-speech with SSML, custom voice and real-time voice agents.

domains.name: Implement information extraction solutions
domains.summary: Officially 10–15% of the exam. Ingesting and enriching content into Azure AI Search with indexers, skillsets and integrated vectorization, querying with hybrid and semantic ranking, and extracting fields from documents and media with Content Understanding analyzers.

scenarios.title: Insurance claims agent with document intake
scenarios.description: An insurer wants an agent that reads claim forms, photos and adjuster notes, extracts fields and routes claims. Expect questions on Content Understanding analyzers, confidence and grounding, PII redaction, function calling, guardrails and keyless access to storage.

scenarios.description: A retailer wants a chat assistant grounded in its product catalogue and policies. Expect questions on Azure AI Search indexing, hybrid and semantic ranking, agentic retrieval and Foundry IQ knowledge bases, groundedness evaluation, quotas and cost.

scenarios.title: Multi-agent IT operations workflow
scenarios.description: An IT team wants several cooperating agents that triage incidents, call tools and escalate to humans. Expect questions on Foundry Agent Service, Microsoft Agent Framework orchestration, MCP and OpenAPI tools, tracing, RBAC and CI/CD for agent deployments.

scenarios.title: Accessible media library with alt text and video analysis
scenarios.description: A publisher wants alt text for images, searchable video summaries and safe generated artwork. Expect questions on Content Understanding for images and video, gpt-image generation and editing, video generation, and visual content policy enforcement.

scenarios.description: A hotel group wants a voice assistant that understands guests in many languages and answers naturally. Expect questions on speech-to-text, text-to-speech and SSML, translation, real-time speech-to-speech agents, custom voice access and language detection.

lessons.title: Choosing models and Foundry services
lessons.summary: How to pick a model family and the right Foundry building block (prompt agent, hosted agent, direct Responses API call, Foundry Tools) for a workload.

sections.heading: The Microsoft Foundry landscape
sections.body:
Microsoft Foundry (formerly Azure AI Studio / Azure AI Foundry) is the platform for building AI apps and agents on Azure. Azure AI services are now branded **Foundry Tools** (for example Azure Language, Azure Speech, Azure Translator and Azure Content Understanding *in Foundry Tools*).

The current resource model is a **single Foundry resource with one or more projects**, replacing the older hub + Azure OpenAI + AI Services combination. Hub-based projects live on in the **Foundry (classic)** portal, but new investment goes to Foundry projects. An existing Azure OpenAI resource can be **upgraded** to a Foundry resource while keeping its endpoint and keys.

You build through the portal, SDKs (Python, C#, JavaScript, Java), the Azure Developer CLI (`azd`), the VS Code extension, or coding agents.

sections.heading: Choosing a model
sections.body:
The **Foundry Models** catalog holds thousands of models from Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and others. Choose by task rather than by "biggest available":

- **Large language models (LLMs)**: broad reasoning, multistep agent work, complex generation.
- **Small language models (SLMs)**: narrow, high-volume or latency-sensitive tasks where a smaller model is good enough and cheaper.
- **Multimodal models**: when inputs or outputs include images, audio or video.
- **Foundry Tools**: purpose-built services (speech, translation, PII detection, document extraction) when a specialised, predictable API beats prompting a general model.

Model names and versions change frequently, so plan around capabilities and evaluate candidates with your own data instead of hard-coding a "latest" model.

sections.heading: Choosing an agent shape
sections.body:
Foundry Agent Service offers a spectrum:

| Option | When to use |
|---|---|
| **Prompt agent** | Declarative instructions + tools, fully managed by Foundry |
| **Voice-based prompt agent** (preview) | Real-time voice through Voice Live |
| **Hosted agent** | You bring code or a container (Microsoft Agent Framework, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK); Foundry manages the endpoint, scaling and Entra identity |
| **Ephemeral agent** | App code calls the Responses API directly with no stored agent |

The agent API is now the **Responses API (Agents v2)** with conversations, items, responses and agent versions, replacing the Assistants-style threads/messages/runs.

sections.heading: Orchestration choices
sections.body: Foundry **workflows** (preview) offered sequential, group chat and human-in-the-loop patterns in a visual designer, but **Foundry is retiring workflows on December 1, 2026**. For new multi-agent orchestration, plan on **Microsoft Agent Framework** deployed as a hosted agent; use Azure Logic Apps if you need a visual designer, or A2A for simple agent-to-agent handoff.

keyPoints: Azure AI services are now Foundry Tools; Azure AI Foundry is now Microsoft Foundry.
New work uses a single Foundry resource with projects; Azure OpenAI resources can be upgraded in place.
Pick prompt agents for managed declarative agents and hosted agents for your own framework code.
Prefer an SLM or a Foundry Tool when it meets the quality bar more cheaply than a large LLM.
Foundry workflows retire on December 1, 2026; plan new orchestration on Microsoft Agent Framework.

gotchas.trap: Always choose the largest LLM for every task.
gotchas.correct: Match the model to the task; SLMs or Foundry Tools are often cheaper and faster for narrow work.

gotchas.trap: Hosted agents mean you must run your own scaling and identity.
gotchas.correct: Foundry manages the endpoint, scaling and Entra identity for hosted agents; you supply the code.

gotchas.trap: Building a new orchestration on Foundry workflows is the long-term path.
gotchas.correct: Workflows retire December 1, 2026; Microsoft recommends Agent Framework as a hosted agent.

lessons.lab: In a Foundry project, browse the model catalog and shortlist one LLM and one SLM for a summarisation task. Create a prompt agent with each, run the same five test prompts in the playground, and compare quality, latency and token use before choosing.

lessons.title: Retrieval, indexing, memory and knowledge
lessons.summary: Designing grounding: classic versus agentic retrieval in Azure AI Search, when vectors are needed, Foundry IQ knowledge bases, and memory versus knowledge versus file search.

sections.heading: Classic search versus agentic retrieval
sections.body:
Azure AI Search supports two retrieval styles:

- **Classic search**: one index, one request, predictable low latency. Good for search boxes, lookups and simple RAG.
- **Agentic retrieval**: a **knowledge base** over one or more **knowledge sources**. An LLM plans the query, runs subqueries in parallel, applies semantic reranking and merges results with citations. Better for complex, multi-part questions across sources, at the cost of extra latency and model calls (and it is region-restricted).

Microsoft notes that "LLMs and agents don't require vectors. Only use them if you need similarity search."

sections.heading: Query types and ranking
sections.body:
Azure AI Search indexes JSON documents and supports full-text (BM25), vector, **hybrid** and multimodal queries. A hybrid query sends `search` and `vectorQueries` in one request; both run in parallel and results merge with **Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)**. The **semantic ranker** reranks the top results. Keyword search still matters for product codes, jargon, dates and names, which is why hybrid plus semantic ranking is a strong default for natural-language RAG.

Ingestion is **push** (upload JSON yourself) or **pull** (indexers from Blob, Cosmos DB, SharePoint, OneLake and more), optionally with skillsets for chunking and embedding.

sections.heading: Foundry IQ
sections.body: **Foundry IQ** is a managed knowledge layer built on Azure AI Search. A knowledge base groups knowledge sources (Blob, SharePoint, OneLake, web; indexed or remote) and has a retrieval reasoning effort of minimal, low or medium. It is permission-aware (ACL sync, Purview labels, the caller's Entra identity), can be shared by many agents, and returns citations.

sections.heading: Memory versus knowledge versus files
sections.body:
Pick the right store for each kind of context:

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| User-specific facts learned over time (preferences, history) | **Memory** (preview) |
| Curated organisational content shared by everyone | **Foundry IQ knowledge base** |
| A document the user hands over during this session | **File search tool** |

Managed memory extracts, consolidates and retrieves memories (user profile, chat summary, procedural). It needs chat and embedding deployments, and currently has **no VNet support**. Guard it against memory poisoning through prompt injection.

keyPoints: Classic search = one index, predictable latency; agentic retrieval = LLM query planning across sources.
Vectors are optional; add them only when you need similarity search.
Hybrid queries merge keyword and vector results with RRF; semantic ranker reranks.
Memory for per-user context, Foundry IQ for shared knowledge, file search for session uploads.
Managed memory has no VNet support and must be protected from memory poisoning.

gotchas.trap: Every RAG solution needs embeddings and a vector index.
gotchas.correct: Microsoft states LLMs and agents do not require vectors; use them only when similarity search is needed.

gotchas.trap: Store curated company policies in agent memory.
gotchas.correct: Memory is for user-specific context; curated content belongs in a Foundry IQ knowledge base.

gotchas.trap: Agentic retrieval is always better than classic search.
gotchas.correct: Agentic retrieval adds LLM calls and latency; classic search fits simple, latency-sensitive lookups.

lessons.lab: Create an Azure AI Search index over a sample document set, run the same question as keyword, vector and hybrid queries, then enable the semantic ranker and compare the top three results each time.

lessons.title: Deployment types, infrastructure and CI/CD
lessons.summary: Choosing Global, Data Zone or regional deployments, standard versus provisioned versus batch, and managing Foundry projects and agents through repeatable delivery.

sections.heading: Deployment categories
sections.body:
Foundry Models deployments come in three categories:

- **Standard** (pay per token).
- **Provisioned** (reserved throughput units, PTU) for low latency variance and predictable throughput.
- **Batch** (asynchronous, about **50% cheaper**, 24-hour target, with its own enqueued-token quota).

A **Developer** type exists only for evaluating fine-tuned models (short lifetime, no SLA). Models on **managed compute** (open-source and custom models) do not use these deployment types.

Microsoft's guidance: "For most workloads, start with Global Standard." It gets new models first, has the lowest price, the broadest regions and the highest default quota.

sections.heading: Data processing location
sections.body:
| Scope | Where inference can run |
|---|---|
| **Global** (GlobalStandard, GlobalProvisionedManaged, GlobalBatch) | Any Azure region |
| **Data Zone** (DataZoneStandard, DataZoneProvisionedManaged, DataZoneBatch) | Within the US, EU (EU Data Boundary) or APAC zone |
| **Standard / Regional Provisioned** | Within the chosen Azure geography |

Data at rest always stays in the resource's geography. Use **Azure Policy** to block deployment SKUs that violate residency rules.

sections.heading: Infrastructure design
sections.body: A Foundry deployment typically combines the Foundry resource and projects, model deployments, and optional bring-your-own resources: storage, **Azure AI Search**, and **Azure Cosmos DB for conversation state**. Prompt agents can use private networking, while hosted agents use a bring-your-own VNet. Each agent can have a dedicated **Entra agent identity**.

sections.heading: Agent versions and delivery
sections.body:
Agent versions are snapshotted automatically so you can roll back. **Publishing** gives an agent a stable, versioned endpoint and can target Microsoft Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot, the Entra Agent Registry or the A2A protocol. The agent lifecycle is Create, Test, Trace, Evaluate, Optimize, Publish, Monitor.

For CI/CD, treat the project like any other workload: define infrastructure and deployments as code (for example with `azd`), run evaluations as a quality gate before publishing a new agent version, and promote tested versions rather than editing production agents by hand.

keyPoints: Start with Global Standard unless residency, latency variance or cost model says otherwise.
Data Zone keeps processing in the US, EU or APAC zone; regional types keep it in one geography.
Batch is asynchronous, about half the price, with a 24-hour target and separate quota.
Provisioned (PTU) is for predictable throughput and low latency variance.
Agent versions are snapshotted for rollback; publishing gives a stable versioned endpoint.

gotchas.trap: Global deployments store your data outside your geography.
gotchas.correct: Global affects where inference is processed; data at rest stays in the geography.

gotchas.trap: Use the Developer deployment type for a low-traffic production app.
gotchas.correct: Developer is only for evaluating fine-tuned models and has no SLA.

gotchas.trap: Open-source models on managed compute pick GlobalStandard or Provisioned.
gotchas.correct: Managed compute deployments do not use the standard/provisioned/batch deployment types.

lessons.lab: Deploy the same model twice in a test project, once as GlobalStandard and once as DataZoneStandard, and note the differences in available regions and quota. Then write an Azure Policy assignment that denies Global deployment SKUs in that subscription and confirm a new Global deployment is blocked.

lessons.title: Quotas, cost and monitoring
lessons.summary: Handling TPM quota and rate limits, controlling cost, and monitoring performance, drift, safety events, grounding quality and index health.

sections.heading: Quota and rate limits
sections.body: Standard deployments are limited by **tokens per minute (TPM)** quota. When you hit the limit, request a quota increase or deploy in another region. Global Standard has the highest default quota. Batch uses a separate enqueued-token quota so offline jobs do not consume your online TPM. Someone who only needs to *view* quota can be given **Cognitive Services Usages Reader** at subscription scope.

sections.heading: Cost levers
sections.body:
- Use **Batch** for offline, non-urgent work (about 50% cheaper).
- Global Standard also supports **Flex processing** (cheaper, tolerates delay) and **Priority processing**.
- Choose **Provisioned** when steady, high utilisation makes reserved capacity worthwhile.
- Pick smaller models where they meet the quality bar.
- Remember that playground evaluations are on by default and billed by consumption.

Exact prices and limits change, so check current pricing pages rather than memorising numbers.

sections.heading: The three observability pillars
sections.body:
Foundry observability has three pillars:

1. **Evaluation**: quality and safety scores from built-in or custom evaluators.
2. **Monitoring**: Azure Monitor **Application Insights** dashboards for tokens, latency, errors and quality scores, with alerts.
3. **Tracing**: OpenTelemetry-based traces of each step (supports LangChain, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, Microsoft Agent Framework).

In production, add **continuous evaluation** on sampled live traffic, **scheduled evaluation to detect drift**, scheduled red teaming, and Azure Monitor alerts.

sections.heading: Grounding quality and index health
sections.body: For RAG, monitor both ends of the pipeline. On the retrieval side, watch data ingestion (indexer or push failures, document counts) and relevance using the **Retrieval** and **Document Retrieval** evaluators. On the answer side, watch **Groundedness** and **Relevance** scores. A drop in groundedness with stable model settings often points to stale or missing index content rather than to the model.

keyPoints: TPM quota errors: request more quota or use another region.
Batch has its own quota and is about 50% cheaper for async work.
Evaluation, Monitoring (Application Insights) and Tracing (OpenTelemetry) are the three pillars.
Scheduled evaluation detects drift; continuous evaluation samples live traffic.
Track retrieval quality and ingestion health, not just model output.

gotchas.trap: Switching to key authentication raises the rate limit.
gotchas.correct: Auth method does not change TPM quota; request more quota or add capacity in another region.

gotchas.trap: Tracing alone tells you when quality drifts over weeks.
gotchas.correct: Drift is caught by scheduled evaluation and alerts; tracing explains individual executions.

lessons.lab: Connect a Foundry project to Application Insights, run a short load of requests against an agent, then open the monitoring dashboard to find token use and p95 latency. Add an alert rule on error rate and schedule a recurring evaluation on a fixed test dataset.

lessons.title: Securing Foundry: identity, RBAC and networking
lessons.summary: Keyless authentication with Entra ID and managed identities, the Foundry RBAC roles, least-privilege agent access and private networking.

sections.heading: Keyless first
sections.body: RBAC applies only with **Entra ID authentication**. Microsoft warns: "If you use key-based authentication instead, the key grants full access without role restrictions." Use Entra ID (keyless) with **managed identities** for apps running in Azure, and disable or avoid keys where possible.

sections.heading: Foundry roles
sections.body:
The Foundry roles were renamed from the Azure AI roles (role IDs unchanged):

| Role | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Foundry User** | Build and use in projects (data plane). Minimum for the user principal **and** for the project's managed identity |
| **Foundry Project Manager** | Manage projects; minimum role to **publish agents** |
| **Foundry Account Owner** | Create accounts and projects and manage models; no data actions (cannot build) |
| **Foundry Owner** | Both control plane and data plane (for example fine-tune *and* deploy) |
| **Foundry Agent Consumer** | Least privilege: call agent endpoints only; can be scoped to a project or a single agent |

Do not use **Azure AI Developer** (it targets ML workspaces/hubs) or other Cognitive Services roles for Foundry. **Cognitive Services Usages Reader** at subscription scope lets someone view quota. The Azure portal assigns Agent Consumer only at account scope; use the CLI for project or agent scope.

sections.heading: Managed identities and data access
sections.body: To let Foundry read your data, grant the Foundry managed identity **Storage Blob Data Reader** on the storage account. Each agent can have its own **Entra agent identity**. MCP and other tools can authenticate with keys, Entra (agent or project managed identity), **OAuth identity passthrough (On-Behalf-Of)**, or no authentication.

sections.heading: Private networking and data control
sections.body: Prompt agents support private networking; hosted agents use **bring-your-own VNet**, and hosted agents can also use network egress controls (preview). You can bring your own storage, Azure AI Search and **Azure Cosmos DB for conversation state** to keep data in resources you control. Check feature limits: managed memory currently has no VNet support.

keyPoints: Keys bypass RBAC entirely; use Entra ID and managed identities.
Foundry User is the baseline for both the user and the project managed identity.
Publishing agents needs at least Foundry Project Manager; fine-tune plus deploy needs Foundry Owner.
Foundry Agent Consumer is the least-privilege role for calling agents.
Grant the Foundry managed identity Storage Blob Data Reader to read external storage.

gotchas.trap: Store the API key in Key Vault and you have least privilege.
gotchas.correct: A key still grants full access with no role restrictions; use Entra ID with RBAC.

gotchas.trap: Assign Azure AI Developer to Foundry developers.
gotchas.correct: Use the Foundry roles; Azure AI Developer covers ML workspaces and hubs.

gotchas.trap: Foundry Account Owner can do everything in a project.
gotchas.correct: Account Owner manages accounts, projects and models but has no data actions.

lessons.lab: Disable key access on a test Foundry resource, give your App Service a system-assigned managed identity, assign it Foundry User, and call a model with DefaultAzureCredential. Then assign Foundry Agent Consumer at agent scope to a second identity using the CLI and confirm it can call only that agent.

lessons.title: Responsible AI: guardrails, evaluations and oversight
lessons.summary: Configuring guardrails and controls, running quality and safety evaluations and red teaming, and keeping humans in control of agent tool use.

sections.heading: Guardrails and controls
sections.body:
A **guardrail** is a named collection of **controls**; it replaces the older "content filter" configuration and uses Azure AI Content Safety classifiers. Each control names a **risk**, the **intervention points** and an **action**.

- **Intervention points**: User input, Tool call (preview, agents), Tool response (preview, agents), Output.
- **Risks**: Hate, Sexual, Self-harm, Violence, User prompt attacks (jailbreak), Indirect attacks (XPIA), Spotlighting (preview), Protected material, Groundedness (preview), PII (preview), Task adherence (preview).
- **Actions**: Annotate (models only) or Annotate and block.

The default guardrail is **Microsoft.DefaultV2**.

sections.heading: Severity thresholds and inheritance
sections.body:
For harm categories the blocking level is the *threshold*:

| Setting | Blocks |
|---|---|
| Low | High only |
| Medium | Medium and high |
| High | Low, medium and high (strictest) |

Only approved customers (via the modified guardrails form) can turn output filtering off. An agent with no custom guardrail inherits its model deployment's guardrail, but **an agent's own guardrail fully overrides the model's guardrail**, so it must include every control you still need.

sections.heading: Evaluations and red teaming
sections.body:
Built-in evaluators cover quality (Coherence, Fluency), RAG (Retrieval, Groundedness, Relevance), risk and safety (Hate and Unfairness, Violence, Indirect Attack, Protected Materials, Code Vulnerability, Sensitive Data Leakage and others), and agents (Task Adherence, Intent Resolution, **Tool Call Accuracy**, Tool Selection and others). Recommended combinations: RAG = Retrieval + Groundedness + Relevance + safety; agents = Output Quality + Tool Use Quality + Rubric + safety.

The **AI red teaming agent** uses Microsoft's **PyRIT** framework to probe for unsafe behaviour, and can run on a schedule after release.

sections.heading: Tracing, provenance and agent oversight
sections.body:
OpenTelemetry **tracing** records every model call and tool call, giving you the provenance trail of how an answer was produced. For oversight of tool use:

- On an **MCP tool**, set `allowed_tools` to the specific tools the agent may use (an empty list `[]` allows **all** tools) and set `require_approval` (for example `"always"`) for tools that write data or change resources. The client receives an `mcp_approval_request` and replies with an `mcp_approval_response`.
- Treat server-supplied tool descriptions as untrusted, and log approvals.
- A **toolbox** centralises a versioned tool set behind one MCP-compatible endpoint with central authentication and toolbox-level guardrails.

keyPoints: Guardrail = collection of controls (risk + intervention points + action); default Microsoft.DefaultV2.
Low blocks only high severity; High is strictest.
An agent guardrail fully replaces the model deployment guardrail.
Use Indirect attack controls on tool responses for agents that read external content.
allowed_tools: [] allows everything; require_approval gates risky tool calls.

gotchas.trap: Setting the threshold to High lets more content through.
gotchas.correct: High is the strictest setting and blocks low, medium and high severity.

gotchas.trap: An agent guardrail adds to the model guardrail.
gotchas.correct: The agent guardrail fully overrides it; copy any controls you still need.

gotchas.trap: Set allowed_tools to an empty list to disable all MCP tools.
gotchas.correct: An empty list allows all tools; list the permitted tool names explicitly.

lessons.lab: Create a custom guardrail that includes an Indirect attacks control at the tool response intervention point, plus the harm-category and PII controls you need (an agent guardrail replaces the model guardrail, so include everything). Attach it to an agent with a web search tool and test with a page containing hidden instructions. Then run the Indirect Attack and Groundedness evaluators on a small dataset and review the traces of flagged runs.

lessons.title: Build generative apps on Foundry: models, deployments and the project client
lessons.summary: Pick the right model and deployment type, connect an app to a Foundry project with keyless auth, and manage conversation state with the Responses API.

sections.heading: Choosing the model
sections.body:
The Foundry Models catalog holds models from Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and others. Match the model to the job:

- **Large language models** for open-ended reasoning, synthesis and agent planning.
- **Small models** when the task is narrow (classification, routing, short extraction) and latency or cost matters more than depth.
- **Code models** for generation, review and refactoring of source code.
- **Multimodal models** when inputs include images or audio alongside text.
- **Reasoning models** when a task benefits from internal multistep thinking; they trade latency and output tokens for quality.

Model names change often. On the exam, reason from the *requirement* (latency, cost, modality, depth) rather than a specific model version.

sections.heading: Deployment types
sections.body:
Deployments fall into three billing categories: **standard** (pay per token), **provisioned** (reserved throughput units) and **batch** (asynchronous, about half the cost of standard, 24-hour target, separate enqueued-token quota).

Data processing location is part of the SKU name:

| Prefix | Where inference may run |
|---|---|
| Global | Any Azure region |
| DataZone | Inside the US, EU or APAC data zone |
| Standard / Regional Provisioned | The chosen Azure geography |

Microsoft's guidance: **for most workloads, start with Global Standard** (new models first, broadest regions, highest default quota). Move to Provisioned for predictable throughput and low latency variance. The Developer type is only for evaluating fine-tuned models.

sections.heading: Connecting an application to a Foundry project
sections.body:
The current SDK pattern is a single unified project client (`azure-ai-projects` 2.x) pointed at the **project endpoint** (`https://<resource>.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/<project>`), authenticated with **Microsoft Entra ID** through `DefaultAzureCredential` or a similar credential. From that client you obtain an OpenAI-compatible client (`get_openai_client()`) for Responses, agents, and evaluations.

- Use keyless (Entra) auth. RBAC only applies with Entra; an API key grants full access without role restrictions.
- Give the calling identity **Foundry User** on the Foundry resource. The project's managed identity needs it too.
- The v1 routes (`/openai/v1/`) replace the old monthly `api-version` pattern.

sections.heading: Conversation state with the Responses API
sections.body:
The Responses API replaces the Assistants API vocabulary: threads, messages, runs and assistants become **conversations, items, responses and agent versions**.

Ways to carry state across turns:

1. **`previous_response_id`** chaining: send only the new user message and pass the prior response ID.
2. **Conversations**: attach turns to a durable conversation object.
3. **Stateless input arrays** (`store=false`): your app appends output items and resends the history each turn.

Stored response data is kept for a limited retention period by default (30 days at the time of writing) and can be deleted by ID.

keyPoints: Start with Global Standard unless you need predictable throughput (Provisioned) or cheap asynchronous work (Batch).
DataZone SKUs keep processing inside the US, EU or APAC zone; Global can process anywhere.
Connect with the project endpoint plus an Entra credential; assign Foundry User.
Key-based auth bypasses RBAC entirely.
Responses API terms: conversations, items, responses, agent versions.

gotchas.trap: Using an API key in an environment variable is "keyless enough" for least privilege.
gotchas.correct: A key grants full access with no role restrictions. Use Entra ID so Foundry RBAC roles apply.

gotchas.trap: Assigning the Azure AI Developer role for Foundry project access.
gotchas.correct: Azure AI Developer targets ML workspaces and hubs. Use the Foundry roles, starting with Foundry User.

gotchas.trap: Batch deployments are for latency-sensitive traffic because they are cheaper.
gotchas.correct: Batch is asynchronous with a 24-hour target; use it only for work that can wait.

Remove your own Foundry User assignment and observe the authorization error.

lessons.title: Implement retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
lessons.summary: Ground model answers in your data with classic RAG (hybrid search plus semantic ranker) or agentic retrieval through Foundry IQ knowledge bases.

sections.heading: Why RAG
sections.body: Models only know their training data and accept a limited number of input tokens. RAG retrieves the most relevant chunks for each question and puts them in the prompt as **grounding data**. The retrieval system must return concise, highly relevant results, not document dumps: extra tokens cost money and degrade quality.

sections.heading: Classic RAG on Azure AI Search
sections.body:
The proven pattern, best when you need GA features and predictable low latency against one index:

- **Ingestion**: push JSON documents, or pull with indexers (Blob, Cosmos DB, SharePoint, OneLake and more). Skillsets handle chunking, embedding, OCR and LLM enrichment; integrated vectorization embeds at index and query time.
- **Hybrid search**: one request with both a text query and vector queries; results are merged with **Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)**.
- **Semantic ranker**: reranks the top results by meaning and returns a reranker score.

Keyword matching still wins for product codes, names, dates and jargon, which is why hybrid beats pure vector for most enterprise content. "LLMs and agents don't require vectors": use vectors when you need similarity search.

sections.heading: Agentic retrieval and Foundry IQ
sections.body:
**Agentic retrieval** uses an LLM to plan the query, splits complex questions into subqueries that run in parallel, reranks semantically, and returns merged results with citations.

**Foundry IQ** is the managed knowledge layer built on it. A **knowledge base** groups **knowledge sources** (Blob, SharePoint, OneLake, web; indexed or remote), has a retrieval reasoning effort (minimal, low or medium), is **permission-aware** (ACL sync, Purview labels, the caller's Entra identity), and can be shared by many agents.

Azure AI Search recommends starting **new** RAG implementations with agentic retrieval, especially for agents, complex or multi-part questions and several sources. Choose classic RAG when you need GA-only features, when simplicity and speed (one request, no LLM query planning) matter most, or when you want to keep existing orchestration code. Note that LLM-based query planning is still marked preview.

sections.heading: Knowledge, memory or files?
sections.body:
| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Curated organizational content shared across users | Foundry IQ knowledge base / Azure AI Search tool |
| A document a user provides during this session | File search tool |
| Facts about a user learned over time | Memory (memory search tool) |

In the prompt, tell the model to answer only from the supplied sources and to **cite them inline**; citations make fabrications easier to spot and less likely.

keyPoints: Hybrid = text + vector in one request, merged with RRF; add semantic ranker for relevance.
Agentic retrieval = LLM query planning, parallel subqueries, semantic reranking, citations.
Foundry IQ knowledge bases are permission-aware and shareable across agents.
File search for session documents, memory for user facts, knowledge bases for curated content.

gotchas.trap: Pure vector search is always the best retrieval for RAG.
gotchas.correct: Exact identifiers and jargon need keyword matching. Use hybrid search with the semantic ranker (classic RAG), or agentic retrieval, which has semantic ranking built in.

gotchas.trap: Stuffing every retrieved document into the prompt improves answers.
gotchas.correct: Token limits and noise degrade quality. Return a small set of highly relevant chunks.

gotchas.trap: Use memory to store the company handbook for all users.
gotchas.correct: Memory is user-specific context. Curated shared content belongs in a knowledge base.

lessons.lab: Index a folder of PDFs in Azure AI Search with integrated vectorization, then compare keyword, vector, hybrid and hybrid-plus-semantic queries for a question that contains a product code. Next, create a Foundry IQ knowledge base over the same content and attach it to a prompt agent; ask a two-part question and inspect the subqueries and citations.

lessons.title: Evaluate models, RAG apps and agents
lessons.summary: Use Foundry built-in evaluators to measure fabrication, relevance, quality and safety, from single turns to whole agent conversations.

sections.heading: Evaluator families
sections.body:
- **General purpose**: Coherence, Fluency.
- **Textual similarity** (needs ground truth): Similarity, F1, BLEU, GLEU, ROUGE, METEOR.
- **RAG**: Retrieval, Document Retrieval, **Groundedness** (LLM judge, 1-5), **Groundedness Pro** (preview; Content Safety-based pass/fail, no model deployment needed), Relevance, Response Completeness.
- **Risk and safety**: Hate and Unfairness, Sexual, Violence, Self-Harm, Protected Materials, **Indirect Attack (XPIA)**, Code Vulnerability, Ungrounded Attributes, Prohibited Actions, Sensitive Data Leakage.
- **Agent**: Task Adherence, Task Completion, Intent Resolution, Task Navigation Efficiency, **Tool Call Accuracy**, Tool Selection, Tool Input Accuracy, Tool Output Utilization, Tool Call Success, plus batched graders (Quality Grader, Output Quality, Tool Use Quality).
- **Custom**: Rubric evaluator (weighted criteria), Azure OpenAI graders, and your own code or prompt evaluators.

sections.heading: Detecting fabrication
sections.body: "Fabrication" maps to **groundedness**: is every claim supported by the retrieved context? Pair it with **Relevance** (does the answer address the question?) and **Retrieval** (did search return the right chunks?). Low groundedness with good retrieval points at the prompt or model; low retrieval points at the index or query.

sections.heading: Recommended combinations
sections.body:
| Scenario | Evaluators |
|---|---|
| RAG | Retrieval + Groundedness + Relevance + safety |
| Agents | Output Quality + Tool Use Quality + Rubric + safety |
| Translation | BLEU + METEOR + Fluency + Coherence |

Evaluations run at **turn** level (default) or **conversation** level; conversation level needs data in the `messages` format.

sections.heading: From development to production
sections.body: Foundry observability has three pillars: **evaluation**, **monitoring** (Application Insights dashboards for tokens, latency, errors and quality scores, with alerts) and **tracing**. After launch, run **continuous evaluation** on sampled live traffic, **scheduled evaluation** to detect drift, and scheduled red teaming with the **AI red teaming agent** (built on PyRIT).

keyPoints: Groundedness detects fabrication; Relevance checks the answer fits the question; Retrieval checks the search step.
Groundedness Pro is pass/fail and needs no model deployment.
Tool Call Accuracy, Tool Selection and Tool Input Accuracy grade agent tool use.
Conversation-level evaluation requires the messages data format.
Scheduled evaluations detect drift; continuous evaluation samples live traffic.

gotchas.trap: BLEU or ROUGE scores tell you whether a RAG answer is grounded.
gotchas.correct: They measure overlap with a reference answer. Use Groundedness for fabrication.

gotchas.trap: Safety evaluation only needs the four harm categories.
gotchas.correct: Agents that read external content also need Indirect Attack (XPIA) and related evaluators, plus red teaming.

lessons.lab: Build a 20-row test set of questions, retrieved context and responses from your RAG app. Run Retrieval, Groundedness, Relevance and Violence evaluators in Foundry, find the lowest-scoring rows, and decide whether each failure comes from retrieval or generation.

lessons.title: Build agents: roles, state, tool schemas, function calling and memory
lessons.summary: Design a Foundry agent with clear instructions, the right conversation-tracking approach, strict tool schemas, client-side function calling and managed memory.

sections.heading: Agent types
sections.body:
- **Prompt agent**: declarative and fully managed (model + instructions + tools).
- **Voice-based prompt agent** (preview): built on Voice Live.
- **Hosted agent**: your own code or container (Microsoft Agent Framework, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK); Foundry manages the endpoint, scaling and Entra identity.
- **Ephemeral agent**: app code calls the Responses API directly.

Lifecycle: Create, Test (playground), Trace, Evaluate, Optimize, Publish (stable, versioned endpoint), Monitor. Versions are snapshotted automatically so you can roll back.

sections.heading: Roles, goals and conversation tracking
sections.body:
Instructions should state the agent's **role**, its **goal**, what it must not do, when to use each tool, and how to respond when it lacks information. Keep instructions specific and testable; the agent optimizer (preview) can later rewrite instructions and tool descriptions against evaluation results.

Conversation tracking: use a **conversation** for durable multi-turn sessions, `previous_response_id` for simple chaining, or your own state with `store=false`. You can bring your own Azure Cosmos DB for conversation state.

sections.heading: Tool schemas and function calling
sections.body:
A function tool has a **name**, **description** and JSON Schema **parameters**. Good descriptions tell the model *when* to call the tool; tight schemas (enums, required fields, `additionalProperties: false`) stop malformed calls.

Function calling is **client-side execution**:

1. The model returns a function call item with a `call_id` and arguments.
2. **Your app** runs the function.
3. Your app sends a `function_call_output` with the same `call_id` in the same conversation.
4. The agent continues with the result.

Submit outputs promptly; pending runs expire (the docs state 10 minutes after creation). Where supported, set `strict: true` (with all fields required and `additionalProperties: false`) so arguments match the schema. Azure OpenAI structured outputs do not support parallel function calls, so set `parallel_tool_calls` to false. Prompt agents that use the Copilot harness reject `strict: true`.

sections.heading: Memory (preview)
sections.body:
Managed long-term memory runs **extraction, consolidation** (an LLM merges duplicates and resolves conflicts) and **retrieval**. Memory types: **user profile** (retrieve at conversation start), **chat summary** (retrieve each turn) and **procedural** (reusable routines).

Attach the **memory search tool** to a prompt agent (scope resolves with `{{$userId}}`) or use the Memory Store APIs. It needs chat **and embedding** deployments and has no VNet support. Guard against **memory poisoning** via prompt injection with prompt shields and adversarial testing.

keyPoints: Prompt agents are declarative; hosted agents run your own framework code.
Function calling: the model requests, your app executes, you return function_call_output with the call_id.
strict: true enforces the schema; disable parallel tool calls with strict structured outputs.
Memory types: user profile, chat summary, procedural.
Memory needs chat and embedding deployments and does not support VNet.

gotchas.trap: Foundry executes your custom function on its servers once you register it.
gotchas.correct: Function calling is client-side. Your application runs the code and returns the output.

gotchas.trap: JSON mode guarantees the arguments match your schema.
gotchas.correct: JSON mode only guarantees valid JSON. Structured outputs with strict: true enforce the schema.

gotchas.trap: Writing "never reveal secrets" in instructions is enough to stop memory poisoning.
gotchas.correct: Use prompt shields and adversarial testing; instructions alone are not a control.

lessons.lab: Create a prompt agent with a get_order_status function tool (strict schema, enum for region). Write the client loop that detects the function call, runs a local stub, and returns function_call_output. Then attach the memory search tool, tell the agent a preference, start a new conversation, and confirm the preference is recalled.

lessons.title: Agent tools, toolboxes and approval flows
lessons.summary: Connect agents to APIs, knowledge, search, Content Understanding and MCP servers, share tools through toolboxes, and put humans in the loop for risky actions.

sections.heading: The tool catalog
sections.body:
Built-in and custom tools include MCP, Web search, Azure AI Search, Code interpreter, File search, **OpenAPI**, Agent-to-agent (A2A), Browser automation, Fabric IQ, Work IQ, Tool search, Skills, **Function calling**, Grounding with Bing, Computer use, Image generation, SharePoint, Fabric data agent, Azure Functions and Memory search.

For document-heavy tasks, call **Azure Content Understanding** (analyzers that return structured fields, Markdown and confidence/grounding) through a custom function or framework integration, then hand the agent structured JSON instead of raw OCR.

sections.heading: Toolboxes and tool search
sections.body:
A **toolbox** is a curated, versioned set of tools exposed through **one managed MCP-compatible endpoint**, with centralized authentication (Entra ID, OAuth passthrough), toolbox-level guardrails, and promote-to-default versioning so agents pick up changes **without redeployment**.

**Tool search** hides a large tool set behind two meta-tools, `tool_search` and `call_tool`, which cuts token cost and improves tool selection.

Some tools are **direct-only** (not available in a toolbox): function calling, Grounding with Bing, computer use, image generation, SharePoint, Fabric data agent and Azure Functions.

sections.heading: MCP tool configuration
sections.body:
Configure `server_label`, `server_url` (or `project_connection_id`), `allowed_tools`, and `require_approval`.

- **`allowed_tools: []` allows every tool, not none.** List tools explicitly.
- With `require_approval: "always"`, the agent emits an `mcp_approval_request` item. Your client sends an `mcp_approval_response` with the `approval_request_id` and approve or deny, in the same conversation.
- Require approval for tools that write data or change resources, treat server-supplied tool descriptions as untrusted, and log approvals.
- Tool auth options: key-based, Entra (agent identity or project managed identity), OAuth identity passthrough, or unauthenticated.

sections.heading: Safeguards for autonomous and semiautonomous agents
sections.body:
Layer the controls:

- **Approval gates** on MCP tools, or human-in-the-loop steps in an orchestration.
- **Guardrails** with agent intervention points: user input, **tool call** and **tool response** (preview), and output. Indirect attack (XPIA) detection on tool responses catches instructions hidden in retrieved content.
- **Least privilege**: a dedicated Entra agent identity per agent and narrow tool scopes.
- **Deterministic limits in code** (amount thresholds, allow lists) for actions where the rules are known.

keyPoints: Toolbox = one MCP-compatible endpoint, central auth, versioned, no agent redeploy.
Tool search uses tool_search and call_tool meta-tools to shrink large tool sets.
Function calling, Bing, SharePoint and Azure Functions are direct-only.
Empty allowed_tools means ALL tools.
Approval flow: mcp_approval_request in, mcp_approval_response with approval_request_id out.

gotchas.trap: Setting allowed_tools to an empty list blocks all MCP tools until you add some.
gotchas.correct: An empty list allows every tool on the server. Name the allowed tools explicitly.

gotchas.trap: Trust the tool descriptions the MCP server provides; they come from the vendor.
gotchas.correct: Treat server-supplied descriptions as untrusted input that could carry injected instructions.

gotchas.trap: Put function tools in a shared toolbox so every agent gets them.
gotchas.correct: Function calling is direct-only. Attach it to each agent.

lessons.lab: Add a remote MCP server to a prompt agent with two allowed tools, one read-only and one that writes. Set require_approval so only the write tool needs approval, trigger it, inspect the mcp_approval_request item, and send a deny response. Then move the read-only tool into a toolbox and attach the toolbox to a second agent.

lessons.title: Multi-agent orchestration, publishing and agent monitoring
lessons.summary: Orchestrate several agents with Microsoft Agent Framework or Foundry workflows, publish versioned agents, and use traces and agent evaluators for error analysis.

sections.heading: Orchestration options
sections.body:
**Foundry workflows** (preview) offer a visual designer plus YAML with three patterns: **Sequential**, **Group chat** (dynamic handoff and escalation) and **Human in the loop** (approvals or clarifying questions). Nodes include Agent, Logic (if/else, go to, for each), Data transformation and Basic chat.

**Foundry is retiring workflows on December 1, 2026.** The recommended replacement is **Microsoft Agent Framework** (declarative YAML or code) deployed as a **hosted agent**. Use Azure Logic Apps when you need a visual designer, and the **A2A** protocol for simple agent-to-agent handoff.

sections.heading: Microsoft Agent Framework
sections.body:
Agent Framework combines **agents** (LLM + tools + MCP), a **harness agent** for long multistep tasks (planning, context compaction, memory, tool approval), **workflows** (functional and graph-based, with explicit execution paths between agents and functions) and **integrations**. Building blocks include model clients, agent sessions for state, context providers for memory, **middleware** to intercept agent actions, and MCP clients.

Explicit graph workflows are the natural home for hybrid designs where some steps are deterministic functions and others are LLM agents.

sections.heading: Publishing and versions
sections.body: Publishing creates a stable, versioned endpoint and can target Microsoft Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot, the Entra Agent Registry and A2A. Versions are snapshotted automatically, so a bad change can be rolled back. Publishing requires at least **Foundry Project Manager**; callers that only invoke the agent need **Foundry Agent Consumer**.

sections.heading: Monitoring and error analysis
sections.body:
Connect **Application Insights** to the project and Foundry records **server-side traces** for prompt agents, hosted agents and workflows with no code changes. Traces capture latency, exceptions, prompt content, tool calls and retrieval operations, using OpenTelemetry semantic conventions.

Error analysis loop:

1. Filter traces for failures or low quality scores.
2. Open the span tree to find the failing step (retrieval miss, wrong tool, bad arguments, tool error, timeout).
3. Score at scale with agent evaluators (Tool Call Accuracy, Tool Call Success, Task Adherence, Intent Resolution).
4. Fix instructions, tool descriptions or schemas, re-evaluate, publish a new version.

keyPoints: Foundry workflows: Sequential, Group chat, Human in the loop; retiring December 1, 2026.
Replacement: Microsoft Agent Framework deployed as a hosted agent.
A2A for simple agent-to-agent handoff; Logic Apps if a visual designer is required.
Server-side tracing needs only a connected Application Insights resource.
Agent evaluators turn trace review into measurable error analysis.

gotchas.trap: Start a new long-lived orchestration in the Foundry workflow designer.
gotchas.correct: Workflows retire December 1, 2026. Build new orchestration with Agent Framework.

gotchas.trap: Hosted agents can be dropped into the workflow designer as nodes.
gotchas.correct: Hosted agents are not supported in the designer; orchestrate them in Agent Framework code.

Deploy it as a hosted agent, connect Application Insights, run five tickets, and use the trace view to find the slowest span.

lessons.title: Optimize: prompts, parameters, reflection, observability and hybrid orchestration
lessons.summary: Tune generation with prompt techniques and parameters, add self-critique loops, measure tokens and latency with tracing, and combine models with deterministic rules.

sections.heading: Prompt engineering
sections.body:
- **System (or developer) message**: role, rules, output format.
- **Few-shot examples**: in chat APIs, add example user and assistant turns after the system message. Examples condition only the current inference; nothing is permanently learned.
- **Grounding data**: the most effective way to get reliable answers for non-creative tasks.
- **Citations**: asking for inline citations reduces fabrication more than "don't make things up".
- **Order matters** (recency bias): content at the end can dominate, so repeating key instructions at the end can help.
- **Output structure**: specify it, or enforce it with structured outputs.

Chain-of-thought prompting applies to **non-reasoning models only**. Reasoning models think internally; do not try to extract raw reasoning (use the reasoning summary parameter).

sections.heading: Model parameters
sections.body:
| Parameter | Effect |
|---|---|
| `temperature` (0-2) | Higher = more varied; lower = focused. Low for legal or factual output. |
| `top_p` | Also controls randomness, differently. Change temperature **or** top_p, not both. |
| `max_output_tokens` / `max_completion_tokens` | Caps total generated tokens. For reasoning models this includes reasoning tokens. |
| `reasoning_effort` | How long a reasoning model thinks; supported values vary by model. |

Reasoning tokens are billed as output tokens, so higher effort costs more even when the visible answer is short.

sections.heading: Reflection, chain-of-thought evaluation and self-critique
sections.body:
A self-critique loop is a pattern you build:

1. **Generate** a draft.
2. **Critique** it against explicit criteria: an evaluator (Groundedness, Relevance, a Rubric evaluator) or a second model call with a scoring rubric.
3. **Revise** using the critique as feedback.
4. **Stop** when the score passes a threshold or after a fixed number of iterations.

Chain-of-thought evaluation means grading the *process* as well as the answer: did the agent take sensible steps, call the right tools with the right inputs, and avoid unnecessary steps (Task Navigation Efficiency, Tool Call Accuracy). Always bound loops; unbounded reflection multiplies cost and latency.

sections.heading: Observability: traces, tokens, latency, safety signals
sections.body:
Server-side tracing (connect Application Insights) covers Foundry-hosted agents with no code changes. Add **client-side** OpenTelemetry instrumentation (`azure-core-tracing-opentelemetry` with the projects SDK) to trace your own code around agent calls. Querying telemetry needs the **Log Analytics Reader** role on the Application Insights resource.

Monitoring dashboards show **token usage, latency, errors and quality scores**, with Azure Monitor alerts. Span-level latency breakdowns reveal whether time goes to retrieval, tool calls or generation. Guardrail annotations and safety evaluator results are the safety signals.

sections.heading: Orchestrating multiple models and hybrid LLM/rules engines
sections.body:
- **Route by difficulty**: a small, fast model for classification or routing, a larger or reasoning model only for hard cases.
- **LLM for language, rules for decisions**: have the model extract structured fields (structured outputs with a strict schema), then let deterministic code apply policy thresholds, eligibility rules or compliance checks. The model can explain the outcome, but it does not make the regulated decision.
- **Explicit execution paths**: Agent Framework graph workflows connect agents and plain functions, so deterministic steps stay deterministic and auditable.

keyPoints: Few-shot examples go after the system message as user/assistant pairs.
Change temperature or top_p, not both; low temperature for factual output.
Chain-of-thought prompting is for non-reasoning models; use reasoning_effort for reasoning models.
Output token caps include reasoning tokens.
Bound every self-critique loop with a threshold and iteration limit.
Use deterministic rules for regulated decisions; use the LLM for extraction and explanation.

gotchas.trap: Add "think step by step" to prompts for reasoning models to improve accuracy.
gotchas.correct: Chain-of-thought prompting is for non-reasoning models. Tune reasoning_effort instead.

gotchas.trap: Set temperature to 0 and top_p to 0.1 together for maximum determinism.
gotchas.correct: Microsoft recommends adjusting one of the two, not both.

gotchas.trap: Let the LLM approve loans as long as the prompt lists the rules.
gotchas.correct: Put hard rules in deterministic code; use the model for extraction and explanation.

lessons.lab: Take a summarization prompt and run it at temperature 0.2 and 1.0; compare variance. Add a critique step that scores each summary with the Groundedness evaluator and revises once if the score is below 4, with a hard limit of two revisions. Trace both versions and compare token totals and end-to-end latency in Application Insights.

lessons.title: Generate and edit images and video
lessons.summary: Use gpt-image models for text-to-image and mask-based edits, and Sora 2 (preview) for asynchronous text, image and video-to-video generation with remix edits.

sections.heading: Image models and the two image APIs
sections.body:
DALL-E 3 (`dall-e-3`) was **retired on March 4, 2026**; existing deployments no longer work. New work uses the **gpt-image** series of models in Foundry Models (some generally available, some limited-access preview). Check the model page for current names rather than hard-coding one.

There are two operations:

- **`images/generations`**: a JSON request that turns a text prompt into one or more images.
- **`images/edits`**: a multipart request that takes one or more input images (PNG or JPG, up to a documented count and size), plus an optional mask, and returns an edited image.

The gpt-image-1 series and gpt-image-2 models **return base64** image data only (no URL option), so plan to decode and store the output yourself.

sections.heading: Inpainting with a mask
sections.body:
To change only part of an image, send a **mask** with the edit request:

- The mask is a **PNG with exactly the same dimensions** as the input image.
- **Fully transparent pixels (alpha 0)** mark the area the model may repaint. The rest of the image is meant to stay as it is, although the docs do not promise pixel-perfect preservation.

A black-and-white JPG or a mask at a different resolution is a common mistake. Describe in the prompt what should appear in the transparent area.

sections.heading: Generation controls
sections.body:
| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| `n` | Number of images per request (a small range, 1–10) |
| `quality` | low / medium / high (newer models add levels); trades cost and latency for detail |
| `size` | Output dimensions; newer models support larger and flexible aspect ratios |
| `output_format` | **PNG (default) or JPEG**. WEBP is not supported |
| `background: transparent` | Requires **PNG** output |
| `output_compression` | 0–100 compression level, used with JPEG output |
| `input_fidelity` | `high` makes the model match the style and features (especially faces) of input images more closely, for subtle edits (not supported on gpt-image-1-mini) |
| Streaming with `partial_images` | Returns progressive previews while the final image renders |

If the prompt is blocked by the deployment guardrail, the call fails with `content_policy_violation`.

sections.heading: Video generation and editing with Sora 2
sections.body:
Sora 2 (preview) supports three modes: **text → video**, **image → video** (the reference image anchors the first frame and **must match the output size exactly**), and **video → video**. It also generates audio.

Video jobs are **asynchronous**: create the job, **poll its status** (for example queued → in progress → completed or failed; the exact status names depend on the API version), then download the result. Typical jobs take minutes, so never hold a user request open waiting for one.

To change a finished clip, use **remix** (reference the completed video's ID, `remix_video_id`) for a targeted edit rather than generating from scratch. Size and duration come from a short fixed set of values, and billing is per second of output.

Sora rejects content not suitable for under-18 audiences, copyrighted characters and music, real people and public figures, and **input images that contain human faces**.

keyPoints: DALL-E 3 is retired; use gpt-image series models.
Edits use images/edits (multipart); generation uses images/generations (JSON).
Mask = PNG, same dimensions as input, transparent pixels mark the editable area.
Transparent background requires PNG; WEBP output is not supported.
input_fidelity high keeps faces and style closer to the input during edits.
Sora 2 is asynchronous: create, poll, download. Remix edits an existing video.
Image-to-video reference images must match the output size exactly.

gotchas.trap: Expecting a URL back from a gpt-image call.
gotchas.correct: gpt-image-1 series and gpt-image-2 models return base64 data only; decode and store it yourself.

gotchas.trap: Painting the edit area black in a JPG mask.
gotchas.correct: Use a PNG of the same size and make the edit area fully transparent (alpha 0).

gotchas.trap: Regenerating a whole video to fix one detail.
gotchas.correct: Use remix with remix_video_id for targeted edits to a completed video.

gotchas.trap: Uploading a photo of a staff member as the Sora reference frame.
gotchas.correct: Input images containing human faces are rejected; use non-face reference media.

Create a same-size PNG mask with a transparent rectangle and call images/edits to replace only that region. If you have Sora 2 preview access, submit a 4-second text-to-video job, poll it until it succeeds, then remix it with a small change.

lessons.title: Visual understanding with Content Understanding
lessons.summary: Extract captions, alt text, categories and structured visual fields from images and video with Content Understanding analyzers, and choose between single-task (standard) and pro-mode pipelines.

sections.heading: Where visual understanding happens
sections.body:
The study guide asks you to implement visual understanding by configuring **Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools**. It runs on the Foundry resource and accepts **documents, images, video and audio**.

For quick, conversational tasks (visual Q&A about one screenshot, a one-off caption) you can send an image to a multimodal chat model. When you need **repeatable, schema-shaped output at scale** (alt text, tags, categories, scene summaries) that downstream systems consume, define a Content Understanding **analyzer**.

sections.heading: Analyzers and field methods
sections.body:
An **analyzer** bundles content extraction settings, a **field schema**, and the **model deployments** it uses. Each field uses one method:

- **extract**: pull a value that literally appears in the content. **Documents only.**
- **classify**: choose from a fixed list of values (for example a product category).
- **generate**: have the model produce a value, such as a caption, alt text or a description of visual characteristics.

In **document analyzers**, turn on **confidence and grounding** (`estimateFieldSourceAndConfidence`) to get a 0–1 confidence score and the source region of each value, so you can route low-confidence results to human review.

Classification across content types lives inside the analyzer as **`contentCategories`** (up to 200). The separate classifier API is deprecated. **Segmentation** (`enableSegment`) splits input by document type or **video scene**.

sections.heading: Prebuilt analyzers for images and video
sections.body:
Start from a prebuilt analyzer when it fits:

- `prebuilt-imageSearch`: image descriptions for search and RAG.
- `prebuilt-videoSearch`: transcripts plus **segment summaries with scene detection**, so you can search a video library by scene.
- Document and audio counterparts (`prebuilt-documentSearch`, `prebuilt-audioSearch`) and layout analyzers such as `prebuilt-layoutWithFigures`.

Since the GA API (`2025-11-01`) you must **bring your own Foundry model deployments** (an LLM plus embeddings) for analyzers that generate or classify; the managed preview capacity is retired. Read and Layout need no LLM.

sections.heading: Single-task versus pro-mode pipelines
sections.body:
The study guide names two pipeline styles:

- **Single-task (standard mode)**: one analyzer, one input, one schema. Use it for most extraction and description jobs.
- **Pro mode** (introduced in the `2025-05-01-preview` API): adds **reasoning across multiple input files** and an **external knowledge base** for linking, enrichment and validation (for example, checking an item against reference data). It was document-focused.

The classic Foundry standard/pro task UI is retired, and newer preview API versions cover similar multi-step ground with **agentic mode**. For the exam, know when the scenario calls for single-input extraction versus cross-file reasoning against reference data.

keyPoints: Content Understanding analyzers take images and video as well as documents and audio.
Field methods: extract (documents only), classify, generate.
Use generate for captions, alt text and visual descriptions; classify for fixed categories.
estimateFieldSourceAndConfidence (document analyzers) returns confidence and grounding for review routing.
prebuilt-videoSearch gives transcripts and scene-segment summaries.
GA requires your own Foundry LLM and embedding deployments.
Pro mode = multiple inputs + reference knowledge + reasoning; standard = single task.

gotchas.trap: Using the extract method for an alt-text field on images.
gotchas.correct: Extract is documents-only; use generate for descriptive fields on images and video.

gotchas.trap: Assuming the service supplies the LLM for analyzers after GA.
gotchas.correct: Bring your own Foundry model deployments and connect them to the analyzer.

gotchas.trap: Choosing pro mode for a simple one-image tagging job.
gotchas.correct: Single-task (standard) analyzers fit single-input jobs; pro mode is for cross-file reasoning with reference data.

Run it on several images and review the generated values. Next, create a document analyzer for a few PDF product sheets with estimateFieldSourceAndConfidence enabled and note which fields fall below a 0.7 confidence threshold. Then run prebuilt-videoSearch on a short clip and inspect the scene segments.

lessons.title: Responsible AI for visual content
lessons.summary: Apply guardrails, Content Safety image analysis, Prompt Shields and custom categories to block unsafe images, defend against text-in-image prompt injection, and enforce watermark and brand policy.

sections.heading: Guardrails on image models and agents
sections.body:
A **guardrail** is a named set of **controls**; each control names a risk, the **intervention points** (user input, output, and for agents tool call and tool response) and an action (annotate, or annotate-and-block). Guardrails replace the older "content filter" configuration and use Azure AI Content Safety classifiers. The default is **Microsoft.DefaultV2**.

Harm-category blocking levels: **Low blocks only high severity, Medium blocks medium and high, High blocks low, medium and high** (strictest). An agent without its own guardrail inherits its model deployment's guardrail, but **an agent's own guardrail fully replaces** the model's. Image generation blocked by a guardrail returns `content_policy_violation`.

Content Understanding inherits the guardrail of the **model deployment** it uses; detections arrive as warnings or errors, and field generation can be withheld while extracted content is kept.

sections.heading: Detecting unsafe or off-brand images
sections.body:
- **Analyze image** in Azure AI Content Safety scores **hate, sexual, violence and self-harm** with severity levels. Use it to screen user uploads or generated images before display.
- **Custom categories (rapid)** (preview) let you define an incident from text and **image** samples, such as prohibited symbols or a misused logo, and include it in an image analysis request to flag policy violations. The standard variant works on text only and retired on September 1, 2026; the rapid variant retires on April 30, 2027, so plan a migration path.
- Content Safety also lists a **content provenance detection** API, which relates to watermark and provenance policy for AI-generated media.

sections.heading: Indirect prompt injection through text in images
sections.body:
A multimodal model reads text that appears inside an image, such as a sign, a screenshot or a scanned page. An attacker can hide instructions there ("ignore previous instructions and..."). This is an **indirect attack** (XPIA), because the instructions come from content rather than from the user.

Defences:

- Turn on the **indirect attacks** control in the guardrail; **Prompt Shields** detects both user prompt attacks and document (indirect) attacks.
- Use **Spotlighting** (preview; models only, not agents) to mark untrusted content so the model treats it as data.
- Treat model output derived from images as untrusted: limit agent tool access and require approval for high-impact actions.

sections.heading: Policy enforcement pipeline
sections.body:
A typical visual policy pipeline:

1. Screen the prompt or upload (guardrail user-input controls, Prompt Shields).
2. Generate or analyze (gpt-image, Sora 2, Content Understanding).
3. Screen the output (guardrail output controls, Analyze image, custom categories (rapid) for symbols and brand rules).
4. Apply provenance or watermark marking according to your policy, and log decisions for audit.

keyPoints: Guardrails = controls (risk + intervention point + action); default Microsoft.DefaultV2.
Medium level blocks medium and high severity; High is the strictest.
Agent guardrail overrides, not merges with, the model guardrail.
Analyze image covers hate, sexual, violence and self-harm.
Custom categories (rapid) flag prohibited symbols and brand rules in images.
Text inside images can carry indirect prompt injection; enable indirect-attack detection.
Content Understanding inherits its model deployment guardrail.

gotchas.trap: Assuming setting the level to High is the most permissive option.
gotchas.correct: High blocks low, medium and high severity; it is the strictest setting.

gotchas.trap: Relying only on user-prompt jailbreak detection for uploaded screenshots.
gotchas.correct: Text in images is indirect input; enable indirect-attack (document) detection, and Spotlighting where the target is a model (it is not supported for agents).

gotchas.trap: Expecting the default harm categories to catch a banned logo.
gotchas.correct: Brand symbols are not a built-in harm category; use custom categories (rapid) with image samples.

lessons.lab: Create a custom guardrail in the Foundry portal with the violence control set to Medium on input and output and the indirect attacks control enabled. Assign it to a vision-capable chat deployment. Upload an image containing printed text that tries to override the system prompt and observe the annotation. Then call Content Safety Analyze image on a sample upload and record the severity it returns for each category.

lessons.title: Text analysis: prompting versus Azure Language
lessons.summary: How to extract entities, topics, summaries and structured JSON, and how to detect sentiment, tone and sensitive content, choosing between generative prompting and Azure Language in Foundry Tools.

sections.heading: Two toolkits for the same job
sections.body:
The AI-103 study guide asks you to extract entities, topics, summaries and structured JSON "by using generative prompting **and** Foundry Tools". Expect questions that make you choose:

- **Generative prompting** with a Foundry model: flexible, handles new entity types, tone and free-form summaries without training, and can return JSON that matches a schema. Output depends on the prompt and model version.
- **Azure Language in Foundry Tools**: task-specific APIs with a predictable response shape, confidence scores and no prompt to maintain.

A good rule: use Azure Language when a prebuilt or custom task exactly fits and you need consistent, auditable output (for example PII redaction). Use an LLM when the schema is bespoke, the task needs reasoning, or the categories change often.

sections.heading: Core versus legacy Azure Language features
sections.body:
Azure Language now splits its features into two groups:

| Group | Features |
|---|---|
| **Core** (recommended for new work) | PII detection (text, conversations, native documents), language detection, prebuilt NER, custom NER, text analytics for health |
| **Legacy** (supported for existing workloads) | sentiment analysis and opinion mining, key phrase extraction, entity linking, summarization (extractive and abstractive), CLU, custom text classification, question answering, orchestration workflow |

So for a **new** solution that needs sentiment, tone, key topics or summaries, the current direction is generative prompting with a Foundry model. Existing workloads on the legacy APIs keep working. Azure Language also offers an MCP server (remote in the Foundry Tool Catalog, or local), so an agent can call Language tasks as tools.

sections.heading: Structured JSON from an LLM
sections.body:
When downstream code parses the output, do not rely on "please answer in JSON" in the prompt. Use **structured outputs**: supply a JSON schema and set `strict: true`, so the model is constrained to return output that matches the schema. The older JSON mode guarantees valid JSON but not adherence to your schema. Keep the schema small, list every field as required (use a null union for optional values), set `additionalProperties: false`, and use enums for fixed label sets (for example `sentiment: positive | neutral | negative`).

Prompting tips that the exam likes:

- Give the label set and definitions in the system message.
- Ask for evidence spans (quotes) next to each extracted value, so a reviewer can check them.
- Use a low temperature for extraction.
- Evaluate the prompt on a labelled sample before going live.

sections.heading: Sensitive content
sections.body:
Two different concerns are often mixed up:

- **PII in the text you process** (names, phone numbers, account numbers). Use Azure Language **PII detection**, which returns categories and a redacted version of the text. Synthetic-replacement anonymization is in preview. Foundry guardrails also list a PII risk (preview) at the model level.
- **Harmful content** (hate, sexual, violence, self-harm) and prompt attacks. That is the job of **Azure AI Content Safety** and Foundry **guardrails**, not Azure Language.

Choose PII detection when the requirement is "remove personal data before storing or indexing"; choose guardrails when the requirement is "block unsafe model input or output".

sections.heading: Domain customisation
sections.body:
When prebuilt results miss domain terms:

- **Custom NER** (core) trains entity extraction on your labelled documents.
- For an LLM, add few-shot examples and a glossary to the prompt, or ground it with retrieval over your domain documents, before you consider fine-tuning.
- **Text analytics for health** is the prebuilt choice for clinical entities and relations.

keyPoints: The study guide expects both generative prompting and Foundry Tools for extraction tasks.
Azure Language core: PII, language detection, prebuilt NER, custom NER, text analytics for health.
Sentiment, opinion mining, key phrases, summarization, CLU and question answering are now legacy in Azure Language.
For machine-parsed output, use structured outputs with a JSON schema and strict: true.
PII detection removes personal data; Content Safety and guardrails handle harmful content and prompt attacks.

gotchas.trap: Building a brand-new sentiment pipeline on Azure Language sentiment analysis because it is the classic answer.
gotchas.correct: Sentiment analysis is now a legacy Azure Language feature. For new work, prefer prompting a Foundry model (with a schema), and keep the legacy API for existing workloads.

gotchas.trap: Asking the model to "reply in JSON" and parsing whatever comes back.
gotchas.correct: Use structured outputs with a JSON schema and strict: true so the response conforms to the schema.

gotchas.trap: Using a Content Safety harm filter to remove phone numbers and names from transcripts.
gotchas.correct: Personal data removal is Azure Language PII detection (or the guardrail PII risk); harm categories do not detect PII.
